clinicalPearls: Early-onset, drug-resistant epilepsy is the hallmark and often the presenting feature, frequently beginning in the first two years of life
Moderate-to-severe intellectual disability with delayed speech and motor milestones is almost universal
A distinctive progressive retinal pigmentary change is characteristic and helps distinguish it from a simple terminal 14q deletion
Microcephaly and relatively non-specific facial features (broad nasal bridge, epicanthic folds, downturned mouth) are common
Recurrent respiratory and other infections point to an accompanying tendency to immune dysfunction
Seizures often persist even when the deleted 14q material is minimal, implicating the ring structure itself rather than gene loss alone
The ring is mitotically unstable, so somatic mosaicism from ring loss or double rings is frequent and can influence severity
reference.pathophysiology: Ring chromosome 14 arises when the two ends of chromosome 14 fuse, usually with loss of the distal segments, to form a circular chromosome. The resulting phenotype reflects both haploinsufficiency of terminal 14q genes and a distinctive ring effect: continuing mitotic instability produces daughter cells with variable ring loss or duplication, generating dynamic tissue mosaicism. Because the severity of the epilepsy correlates poorly with the amount of deleted material, disruption of chromosome architecture and unstable copy number, rather than loss of a single gene, are thought to drive the neurological picture.
additionalDifferentials: Terminal 14q deletion syndrome without a ring
Early-infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathies of single-gene origin
Angelman syndrome and other syndromic epilepsies
Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, given the combination of epilepsy and retinopathy
additionalInvestigations: Conventional karyotype to identify the ring and assess the degree of mosaicism
Chromosomal microarray to define any deleted segment, recognising it may not reveal the ring configuration itself
MRI of the brain for structural anomalies
Ophthalmological assessment including detailed retinal examination
Immunological review and infection surveillance where recurrent infections occur
redFlags: Refractory seizures or episodes of status epilepticus
Progressive visual impairment from retinal degeneration
Recurrent or severe infections raising concern about immune dysfunction
reference.prognosis: Epilepsy is frequently lifelong and difficult to control, and most affected individuals have significant intellectual disability; life expectancy is variable and influenced by the seizure burden, infections, and any associated malformations.
pitfalls: Relying solely on microarray, which may detect a terminal deletion but miss the ring configuration and its instability
Underestimating somatic mosaicism when only a small number of cells is analysed
Attributing seizure severity purely to deletion size and overlooking the ring-specific effect
Missing progressive retinopathy because vision is hard to assess in a child with intellectual disability
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Gardner and Sutherland's Chromosome Abnormalities and Genetic Counseling
management: Control the drug-resistant epilepsy with antiepileptic drugs, escalating to combination regimens, as it is the dominant clinical problem
Provide early developmental intervention with speech, physical and occupational therapy and special education for the intellectual disability
Ophthalmological surveillance for the progressive retinal pigmentary change
Immunological review and infection surveillance for the recurrent respiratory and other infections
Serial EEG and brain MRI to characterise seizures and structural anomalies
Coordinated neurology, clinical genetics and paediatric care
Genetic counselling with parental karyotyping, noting that ring chromosomes usually arise de novo with a low recurrence risk
